note: A specialist society position on AI Act implementation in medical imaging, covering literacy, sandboxes and post market monitoring.
title: Guiding AI in radiology: ESR's recommendations for effective implementation of the European AI Act
explain_beginner: Hospitals increasingly use AI to help read X-rays, CT scans, and other medical images, and Europe's AI Act now regulates that use, but exactly how the law should apply to radiology in practice was unclear, so the European Society of Radiology wrote this position paper to spell it out. It raises a specific worry, an AI tool that quietly rewrites a radiology report using a general purpose language model might not be officially classified as high risk even though a wrong rewrite could mislead a doctor, while a tool that decides which patients' scans get looked at first probably should be high risk because getting that wrong could delay care unfairly for some patients over others. The society also warns that as AI takes on more of the workload, radiologists may start trusting it too much or letting their own skills atrophy, and it flags that nobody yet has a good system for catching an AI imaging tool that quietly gets worse after it is deployed in a real hospital.
explain_business: Hospitals, radiology departments, and imaging AI vendors operating in the EU get a concrete preview of compliance friction points from this statement rather than having to wait for enforcement guidance, specifically that risk classification for report drafting versus triage tools is genuinely unsettled, that post market monitoring for image based AI has no established methodology yet, and that regulatory sandbox access needs to work for small vendors, who dominate this market, not just large corporations. The practical near term step the statement recommends is investing in staff AI literacy and monitoring infrastructure ahead of firm regulatory guidance rather than waiting for it, since the society itself is pushing the European Commission for clarifying use case examples within 18 months rather than reporting that clarity already exists. Vendors and hospitals planning imaging AI rollouts now should budget for this ambiguity directly, including an unresolved question of whether separate patient consent for AI involvement will eventually be required.
explain_practitioner: This ESR position statement synthesizes expert input to identify implementation gaps in applying the EU AI Act to radiology AI, flagging that risk classification is ambiguous at the edges, general purpose AI used for report drafting could evade high risk classification despite hallucination risk, while triage tools prioritizing imaging cases arguably warrant high risk status due to discrimination risk, and recommends the European Commission publish concrete high risk and non high risk use case examples within 18 months. On post market monitoring, the statement argues no standard practice yet exists for detecting model or data drift in deployed imaging AI, that patient level harm can surface months later with unclear causal attribution, and that individual radiology departments lack the resources to monitor this alone, proposing the European Health Data Space as shared infrastructure instead. It is also explicitly skeptical of Article 57 regulatory sandboxes for imaging AI, arguing that real validation needs large multi centre trials the sandbox model was not built for. As a professional society position statement rather than empirical research, several issues it raises, including whether AI use requires separate patient consent, are explicitly left unresolved by the authors themselves.
